resources.string: Signed by %1$s. The signature is valid, but the key only arrived by email and has not been confirmed yet.
The signature is valid, but the key belongs to %1$s, not to the sender %2$s.
Caution: the signature is invalid. The content was changed after signing, or the signature is forged.
Signed by %1$s with an expired key.
Signed by %1$s with a revoked key – no longer trustworthy.
Signed with an unknown key (%1$s). The sender\'s email provider does not publish one.
The email is signed, but the signature cannot be read.
Only part of the email is signed.
The sender\'s OpenPGP key has been saved (not confirmed yet).
Compare the fingerprint with the sender, e.g. by phone: %1$s. Does it match?
Will be signed with OpenPGP – tap to not sign
With your own key you sign your emails. Recipients can then see that they really come from you and were not changed on the way. The private key is stored encrypted on your dmOffice server.
Creates an Ed25519 key (with Curve25519 for encryption).
Paste the private key, e.g. from “gpg --export-secret-keys --armor”. dmOffice stores it without the password, protected by the encryption of your data on the server.
The account\'s address is not in this key – recipients will not see the signature as matching.
Attach public key to signed emails
This account will no longer be able to sign. Anyone who already has your public key can still verify old emails. Without a backup, the private key cannot be restored.

To verify your signature, others need your public key – as an attachment, via Autocrypt or from a directory. Upload it to keys.openpgp.org and confirm your address there, or publish it in the Web Key Directory (WKD) of your domain.
dmOffice takes senders\' public keys from attached keys and Autocrypt headers. Keys from an email only count as verified once you confirm the fingerprint.
Look up at the email provider (WKD)
Only for signed emails with an unknown key, never for junk, at most once a day per sender. The sender\'s provider learns that the email was opened.
